transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-18
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~47 minutes
Recording: auto
Attendees: Alex Park (Redwood AE), Sofia Ramirez (Redwood SE), Matt Johnson (Apex Head of ML), Priya Shah (Eng Manager), Daniel Li (SRE), Karen Yu (Product)

Summary:
Quick discovery focusing on latency and throughput targets for chat completion use-case. Apex wants p95 latency targets for user-facing chat (<300ms if possible), concurrency ~50-100 concurrent users, streaming required, and an objective to benchmark tokens/sec across hosted vs dedicated vs private deployments. Discussed model families, batch sizing, kv cache and quantization tradeoffs, and next steps to run end-to-end benchmarks on H100/A100.

Topics:
- p95 targets and realistic expectations
- concurrency and peak vs sustained QPS
- streaming behavior and per-token latency vs final completion latency
- benchmarking methodology and sample prompt set
- security/compliance: VPC, KMS, SOC2
- cost vs latency tradeoffs (hosted vs dedicated vs private)
-
00:00 Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm alex from redwood inference, i'll run quick intro then hand to sofia for the deep questions.
00:14 Matt: hi alex, thanks, i'm matt. we are trying to understand the latency economics, we have a live chat product and want to move model inference off our prototype infra. p95 goals are tricky for us.
00:25 Alex: totally, that's the core ask. two quick things: is streaming required for your UX? and what's your concurrency target?
00:33 Priya: streaming is required, users start seeing partial answers. target concurrency is around 50 concurrent active chats, planning for bursts to 120.
00:45 Sofia: okay great. when you say p95, are you measuring from request arrival to first token, or to final token? those differ a lot.
00:58 Matt: good point — we measure end-to-end to first token for perceived latency. ideal p95 < 300ms, stretch goal 200ms but we know that's aggressive.
01:10 Sofia: good to clarify. for first-token p95 at 50 concurrent with streaming, that mapsto different stack choices. hosted api typically has variability; dedicated reserved capacity gives more predictable tails.
01:26 Daniel: on infra — we're running on GCP today, but open to dedicated instances. network egress and company firewall rules are strict; we might need a VPC or private deployment.
01:40 Alex: noted. we support hosted, dedicated, and private (VPC/on-prem). we'll capture the constraints. for benchmarks we can run on H100-backed dedicated pools or host runs on our hosted fleet.
01:55 Sofia: quick follow on concurrency: are these 50 independent users each making a request every 10s, or bursts of many parallel requests?
02:05 Priya: mix — average qps per user low but bursts create spikes to ~120 concurrent inflight requests.
02:15 Sofia: got it, so burst capacity and autoscaling behavior matters. we'll include burst tests.

02:45 Matt: what about token/sec metrics — our prompts are typically 512 tokens context and responses ~80 tokens; we care about tokens/sec for cost and throughput.
02:58 Sofia: okay typical metrics to capture: tokens/sec (system-wide), latency per token during streaming, and end-to-end first-token p95. we'll instrument both per-request and aggregated tokens/sec.
03:12 Alex: also note that model size and quantization changes latency — running a 13B quantized model vs 70B fp16 will change per-token latency significantly. we should align on model family.
03:30 Matt: currently prototyping with a 13B open model, might move to 70B if quality requires it. 13B gives better latency but quality holes for some prompts.
03:44 Sofia: for 13B on H100 we typically see first-token p95 in the 150-350ms range depending on batch sizing and KV cache hit rates; but large models will be higher.
03:58 Daniel: what about batching? we worry batching adds tail latency for interactive UX.
04:08 Sofia: correct — batching increases throughput but can add queuing delay. Redwood's continuous batching has small micro-batch windows and can prioritize latency-bound requests; we can configure max batch wait times and per-route latency SLOs.
04:26 Matt: and for streaming, tokens/sec is basically token generation throughput; how do we separate generation time vs network?
04:36 Alex: we'll measure both: model generation time (server-side tokens/sec) and end-to-end including network/streaming chunking. for streaming we often chunk every N tokens and send partials — that influences perceived latency.
04:50 Priya: can you run benchmark with our prompt set and show hosted vs dedicated vs private numbers?
04:57 Sofia: yes. typical plan: you provide prompt set and target concurrency patterns, we run three runs — hosted fleet, dedicated pool (H100), private deployment simulation (if you can host, or we run internal sim with same infra) — report p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, and cost per 1M tokens estimate.
05:16 Matt: timeline? we need results before exec review next week.
05:22 Alex: we can aim to run a first-pass benchmark by 2026-03-20 if prompt set and IP allow, then follow-up review week of 2026-03-23.

06:00 Sofia: two more technical notes: KV cache warmup heavily affects p95 for repeated context. if you have many users reusing similar context we can show big wins. also prefix caching for system prompts.
06:14 Daniel: our sessions often reuse system prompt and a user instruction — maybe 40% cache hit expected. will that reduce p95?
06:20 Sofia: yes, cache hits reduce per-token compute and the effective first-token latency. we'll include warm and cold cache scenarios.

06:50 Matt: security — we require SOC2, SSO (SAML), and audit logs. also KMS integration for customer-managed keys if private.
06:58 Alex: we have SOC2, SAML/SSO support, and KMS/HSM integrations for private deployments. we'll send the security pack.
07:10 Priya: for private deployment, what network topology? we need control plane in our VPC and workers on customer subnets?
07:18 Sofia: for Redwood Private we can deploy control plane with customer-managed networking; workers can be in your VPC or on-prem. we have templates for VPC routing, allowed IP ranges, and firewall rules.
07:30 Daniel: latency on private would be lower network-wise, but ops overhead is a concern.
07:36 Alex: yes, private often reduces network jitter but you trade operational burden - we offer a managed package to reduce that.

08:00 Matt: competition - we've evaluated anthopic and openai; we've also run some in-house tests. their tail behavior varies. what differentiates redwood for us?
08:12 Alex: two quick diffs: 1) production-first controls (batching/caching/policies) to tune latency vs cost; 2) unified experience across hosted/dedicated/private so you can start on hosted then migrate with minimal changes. we'll include examples in the follow-up doc.

09:00 Sofia: benchmark specifics we'll capture: request pattern (poisson vs burst), prompt/context lengths (you said 512/80), concurrency profile (sustained 50, peaks 120), model variants (13B quantized, 13B fp16, 70B fp16), hardware (A100/H100), cache warm/cold, streaming chunk size.
09:25 Priya: chunk size — we send partials at ~16 token chunks. should benchmark with same chunking.
09:32 Sofia: noted. that affects per-token latency and perceived throughput.

10:12 Matt: what about per-route SLO enforcement? can we pin a chat route to dedicated pool?
10:20 Alex: yes, you can route by policy; high-priority routes can be pinned to dedicated capacity. fallback policies exist to send to hosted fallback if dedicated is saturated but you can opt out.
10:35 Daniel: curious about autoscaling for dedicated — how quickly does it scale?
10:42 Sofia: typical autoscaling is sub-minute for adding GPUs (depends on pool config). for extremely tight tail we recommend some reserved headroom and burst capacity options. we'll show charts.

11:05 Priya: cost question — what's unit cost delta between hosted and dedicated?
11:12 Alex: high level: hosted simpler but can be ~20-40% higher per-token at scale because of multi-tenancy overhead; dedicated costs more upfront but wins at sustained high QPS with predictable latency. we'll provide a sample cost model with numbers based on your concurrency and token volume.

12:00 Matt: one more — how do you measure tokens/sec across multi-GPU parallelism?
12:08 Sofia: we measure aggregate tokens/sec as total produced tokens over time, and also per-GPU token throughput; distributed models (model parallel) will have different scaling properties. in our reports we'll show tokens/sec and normalized per-GPU numbers.
12:20 Matt: perfect.

35:00 (later in call - summarizing) Alex: quick recap — matt to send prompt set and clear p95 definition (first-token), daniel to send network constraints, we will run benchmarks (hosted, dedicated H100, private sim) and share results + cost spreadsheet. follow-up week of 3/23.
35:30 Priya: one more ask — include cold start numbers and real-user like jitter.
35:40 Sofia: will do, cold/warm and burst tests included.
